title: The Altar of Witness
overview: Joshua 22 recounts the return of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh to their allotted lands east of the Jordan after helping their brethren conquer Canaan. Joshua commends their faithfulness and sends them home with blessings and spoils. However, conflict arises when these tribes build a large altar near the Jordan, causing alarm among the other Israelites who fear rebellion against God. A delegation led by Phinehas confronts them, but the eastern tribes explain the altar’s purpose as a witness to their shared faith and unity, not for sacrifices. The chapter highlights themes of obedience, unity, and the importance of clear testimony in the community of God. It underscores God’s faithfulness in granting rest and the need for trust and communication among His people.
structure:
**Verses 1-9: Joshua’s Commission and Blessing.** Joshua calls the eastern tribes, commends their obedience, and sends them back to their land with blessings and spoils from the conquest. This section establishes their faithfulness and God’s fulfillment of His promises.

**Verses 10-12: The Altar Built and Israel’s Alarm.** The tribes build a large altar by the Jordan, which causes misunderstanding and fear among the western tribes, who perceive this as potential rebellion and prepare for war.

**Verses 13-20: The Confrontation.** A delegation led by Phinehas confronts the eastern tribes, accusing them of turning away from the LORD by building an altar for sacrifices, referencing past sins like Peor and Achan as warnings.

**Verses 21-29: The Explanation and Reconciliation.** The eastern tribes clarify the altar’s purpose as a witness to unity and shared worship, not for sacrifices, to prevent future division. Their explanation satisfies the delegation.

**Verses 30-34: Peace Restored and Naming the Altar.** Phinehas and the leaders accept their explanation, peace is restored, and the altar is named Ed, meaning witness, symbolizing unity and shared faith.

keyVerses.text: But take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law, which Moses the servant of the LORD charged you, to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways, and to keep his commandments, and to cleave unto him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates the core exhortation to wholehearted obedience and love for God, emphasizing the covenantal faithfulness expected of the tribes. It connects to the chapter’s theme of obedience and loyalty to God’s commands.

keyVerses.text: And when they came unto the borders of Jordan, that are in the land of Canaan, the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by Jordan, a great altar to see to.
keyVerses.significance: This verse introduces the central conflict of the chapter—the building of the altar by the eastern tribes. It highlights the potential for misunderstanding and division within God’s people when actions are unclear.

keyVerses.text: The LORD God of gods, the LORD God of gods, he knoweth, and Israel he shall know; if it be in rebellion, or if in transgression against the LORD, (save us not this day,)
keyVerses.significance: This verse expresses the eastern tribes’ appeal to God’s omniscience and justice, affirming their innocence and trust in God’s judgment. It underscores the importance of integrity and accountability before God.

keyVerses.text: But that it may be a witness between us, and you, and our generations after us, that we might do the service of the LORD before him with our burnt offerings, and with our sacrifices, and with our peace offerings; that your children may not say to our children in time to come, Ye have no part in the LORD.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the true purpose of the altar—as a symbol of unity and shared worship to prevent future divisions. It highlights the importance of testimony and remembrance in the community of faith.

keyVerses.text: And the children of Reuben and the children of Gad called the altar Ed: for it shall be a witness between us that the LORD is God.
keyVerses.significance: The naming of the altar 'Ed' (witness) signifies reconciliation and mutual recognition of God’s sovereignty. It concludes the chapter with a lasting symbol of peace and unity among the tribes.

characters.name: Joshua
characters.description: The leader of Israel who commissions the eastern tribes to return to their land. He blesses them and encourages obedience to God’s law, demonstrating his role as a faithful servant and mediator of God’s covenant.

characters.name: Phinehas
characters.description: Son of Eleazar the priest, he leads the delegation to confront the eastern tribes about the altar. His role as priest and leader is pivotal in resolving the conflict peacefully through investigation and dialogue.

characters.name: Children of Reuben, Gad, and half tribe of Manasseh
characters.description: The tribes who built the altar east of the Jordan. Their motivation was to maintain unity and testimony with the rest of Israel, not rebellion. They demonstrate faithfulness and concern for future generations.

characters.name: The Congregation of Israel
characters.description: The western tribes who initially perceive the altar as an act of rebellion. Their reaction shows the importance of unity and proper worship in Israel and the dangers of misunderstanding.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes the necessity of following God’s law wholeheartedly, as Joshua commands and the eastern tribes affirm. Obedience is foundational for blessing and unity among God’s people.

The altar controversy reveals the importance of maintaining unity among the tribes of Israel. The resolution demonstrates how communication and understanding preserve fellowship within the covenant community.

The altar serves as a witness between the eastern and western tribes, symbolizing their shared faith in God. This theme highlights the need for visible signs to remind future generations of God’s covenant.
The tribes appeal to God’s knowledge and justice to vindicate their actions, trusting in His faithfulness. The chapter underscores that God sees the heart and judges rightly.

historicalContext: Joshua 22 is set in the late Bronze Age, shortly after the Israelites’ conquest of Canaan under Joshua’s leadership, around the 13th century BC. The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh had been granted land east of the Jordan River, in the region of Gilead and Bashan, territories previously inhabited by Amorite peoples. The political situation involved consolidating tribal territories and maintaining unity among the twelve tribes of Israel, who were transitioning from a nomadic to a settled lifestyle. Building altars and places of worship was central to Israelite religious practice, but centralization of worship at the tabernacle was crucial to prevent idolatry and division. The cultural context included strong tribal identities and concerns about inheritance and covenant fidelity.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed interpreters emphasize the chapter’s focus on covenant obedience and unity under God’s law. The altar is seen as a legitimate witness to the unity of God’s people, not a rival sanctuary, highlighting the importance of doctrinal clarity and communal harmony.

Dispensationalists often highlight the literal fulfillment of God’s promises to the tribes and the significance of territorial boundaries. The altar incident is interpreted as a test of faithfulness and a foreshadowing of future divisions in Israel’s history.

Early Church Fathers viewed the altar as a symbol of the unity of the Church and the importance of avoiding schism. They often allegorized the altar as representing the unity of faith and the need for peace among believers.

crossReferences.connection: Echoes Joshua 22:5’s command to love the LORD with all heart and soul, emphasizing wholehearted devotion to God’s covenant.
Solomon’s prayer at the temple reflects concerns about sin, rebellion, and God’s justice, similar to the fears expressed by Israel regarding the altar.
Encourages believers not to forsake assembling together, paralleling the theme of unity and communal worship highlighted by the altar as a witness.
Celebrates the blessing of unity among God’s people, resonating with the reconciliation and peace restored in Joshua 22.
God’s instructions on building altars ‘to the LORD’ provide background for understanding the significance and potential controversy of the altar built by the eastern tribes.

application: Commit to wholehearted obedience and love for God in daily life, as commanded in Joshua 22:5.
Seek unity and clear communication within the church to prevent misunderstandings and divisions.
Use tangible reminders of faith, like testimonies or symbols, to encourage future generations in the knowledge of God.
Trust in God’s justice and omniscience when facing accusations or misunderstandings.
Approach conflicts within the Christian community with humility and a desire for reconciliation.
Remember that God honors sincere motives and faithfulness over mere outward appearances.
conclusion: Joshua 22 powerfully illustrates the challenges and blessings of covenant faithfulness within God’s people. It teaches that obedience, unity, and clear testimony are vital for maintaining fellowship and peace. The chapter’s resolution through dialogue and trust in God’s justice encourages believers to pursue reconciliation and uphold the witness of God’s covenant across generations. For Christians today, it is a reminder that faithfulness involves both heart devotion and communal harmony, grounded in the knowledge that God sees and judges rightly.
